title: Elephants: The Best Animals?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore elephants: the three recognized species (African bush, African forest, Asian) and how they differ in size, tusks, and toes; lifespans in zoos versus timber camps in Burma; diet, digestion, and elephant-dung paper; the trunk; swimming; the Elephant Voices gesture database; the Jenny and Shirley reunion; mirror test and third-party relationship tests of self-awareness; the Happy elephant habeas corpus case; male and female social structure and matriarchs; grief and PTSD; ethics of elephant rides and sanctuaries; and threats from poaching for ivory and skin and habitat loss. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about Robert Moses from the earlier Central Park episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and ethics of elephant interaction
segments.summary: Hosts express their love of elephants and note that writing, bathing with, or riding elephants is unethical because wild elephants are broken through cruel training, including the 'crushing their spirit' process.

segments.title: Elephant species and how they differ
segments.summary: The hosts explain that there are three species: African bush, African forest, and Asian elephants. They compare tusks, toe counts, ear size, head and back shapes, and tusk dominance, and note that forest elephants are elusive and poorly studied.

segments.title: Elephant size and lifespan
segments.summary: Shoulder heights and weights for each species are given, along with notes on size variation and the record Asian elephant. Wild elephants can live 50 to 70 years, with one recorded at 86, while zoo elephants live much shorter lives, based on an RSPCA study. Burma timber elephants are described as living longer and receiving care.

segments.title: Break and banter
segments.summary: Hosts take a break and joke about travel safety and a podcast about their wives.

segments.title: Elephant diet, digestion, and dung
segments.summary: Elephants eat 100 to 600 pounds of food and drink 16 to 40 gallons of water daily, spending most of their waking hours foraging. Their inefficient digestion produces dung used to make paper, and dung can indicate age and size.

segments.title: Elephant range, swimming, and the trunk
segments.summary: Range maps cover Africa and Asia. Elephants swim and float well, and one was recorded swimming 30 miles. The trunk combines nose and upper lip, has many muscles, holds water, and is used for feeding, bathing, and communication.

segments.title: Elephant gestures, intelligence, and reunions
segments.summary: The Elephant Voices gesture database documents elephant communication, including the flop trunk on head play gesture. Baby elephants suck their trunks. Jenny and Shirley, who met in a circus 23 years earlier, reunited with strong excitement.

segments.title: Self-awareness: mirror test and third-party relationships
segments.summary: The mirror test (developed by Gordon Gallup Jr.) is described, with elephant Happy passing it, and dogs not passing. Third-party relationship experiments show elephants recognize kin relationships. The Non-Human Rights Project sought a habeas corpus for Happy, held at the Bronx Zoo.

segments.title: Male and female social structure
segments.summary: Males leave their families as young teenagers and live mostly alone, forming hierarchies when grouped. Musth is described as a state of high testosterone that causes males to be aggressive. Females live in family groups led by a matriarch chosen for experience, and families help each other babysit.

segments.title: Communication, grief, PTSD, and humor
segments.summary: Elephants communicate through rumbles, trumpets, ear flicks, and feet stomping; they sense vibrations and smell water and storms far away. A researcher describes elephant pratfalls as play. Elephants grieve their dead and can suffer PTSD after witnessing violence.

segments.title: Ethics of elephant rides, sanctuaries, and animal interaction
segments.summary: The hosts advise against rides and bathing with elephants, cautioning that 'sanctuary' is not regulated. Maria Mossman of Action for Elephants UK is quoted on unnatural behavior. They mention a viral video of a dog and an elephant.

segments.title: Poaching, ivory and skin trade, and population decline
segments.summary: Elephant populations are declining from habitat loss and poaching for tusks and, newly since 2013, for skin used in jewelry. Burma skin kills rose from 10 in 2012 to 61 in 2016. Legal ivory trade remains in several countries. African elephant numbers fell from about ten million in 1930 to about 415,000 today.

segments.title: Elephants and the human cuteness myth
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a debunked viral claim that elephants find humans cute, noting it was made up and referencing a Snopes article.

segments.title: Listener mail: correction on Robert Moses
segments.summary: A listener named Joe Kennedy writes that Robert Moses had a troubling effect on racial and socioeconomic segregation, and the hosts agree to research further, acknowledging a correction to the earlier Central Park episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, invite feedback through the website and email, and close the episode.
